# Training a behaviour classifier {#sec-classification}

::: {.callout-important title="Skeleton chapter"}
This chapter is currently a **skeleton**: section titles with a short description of
what will go in each, and indicative (not yet runnable) code stubs. It will be
fleshed out into a full tutorial.
:::

In @sec-boris we used BORIS to annotate `mount` events on the video
`mouse044_task1_annotator1.mp4`. In this chapter we put those annotations to work:
we train a **supervised behaviour classifier** that learns to flag `mount` frames
automatically from features derived from the pose tracks.

Make sure you have the `animals-in-motion-env` environment activated (see
[prerequisites @sec-install-movement]), including `scikit-learn`. You will need the
SLEAP predictions (`mouse044_task1_annotator1.slp`) and the BORIS ground-truth
annotations (`mouse044_task1_mount_events_boris.tsv`) from earlier chapters.

::: {.callout-note title="Manage expectations"}
The goal here is to teach the **workflow and the main concepts**, not to train a
production-grade classifier. We deliberately use a single annotated video and a
handful of interpretable features. A good model would need far more data, as we
discuss at the end.
:::

## The pipeline

Structurally this is the same supervised loop as pose estimation (@sec-workflow-sleap)
and behaviour annotation (@sec-boris): select data, label, train, predict. Here the
labels are behaviour states and the features come from the pose tracks.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    poses[/Pose tracks/] --> feat[Kinematic features]
    boris[/BORIS labels/] --> labels[Per-frame labels]
    feat --> train
    labels --> train[Train random forest]
    train --> eval[Evaluate on validation]
    eval --> test[Test on a new video]
```

## Load pose tracks and annotations

Load the pose tracks into a `movement` dataset (as in @sec-movement-load) and the
BORIS aggregated-events TSV into a pandas DataFrame (as in @sec-boris).

```{.python}
# Pose tracks (from SLEAP)
ds = load_dataset(slp_path, source_software="SLEAP", fps=30)

# BORIS annotations (aggregated events: one row per mount bout)
boris_df = pd.read_csv(tsv_path, sep="\t")
```

## Attach annotations as per-frame labels

BORIS gives us one row per `mount` bout, with a start and stop frame. To use these
as training labels we expand them into a **per-frame boolean array** aligned to the
dataset's `time` dimension (`True` while a mount is ongoing), and attach it as a
coordinate. This mirrors the [`movement` "Annotate and load events with BORIS"
example](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/examples/advanced/annotate_boris_events.html).

```{.python}
# Build a per-frame boolean label from (start_frame, stop_frame) intervals
is_mount = np.zeros(ds.time.size, dtype=bool)
for _, ev in boris_df.iterrows():
    is_mount[ev["Image index start"]:ev["Image index stop"]] = True

ds = ds.assign_coords(is_mount=("time", is_mount))
```

This `is_mount` array is our label vector `y`.

## Clean the tracks

Briefly filter low-confidence points, interpolate short gaps, and smooth, exactly as
in @sec-movement-filtering. Clean tracks give cleaner features.

```{.python}
# filter_by_confidence -> interpolate_over_time -> rolling_filter (see @sec-movement-intro)
```

## Compute kinematic features

We derive a small set of **interpretable** features, each motivated by what mounting
looks like in the resident–intruder assay. Keeping the set small and meaningful makes
the model easy to reason about and to plot.

| Feature | `movement` function | Why it should help |
|---|---|---|
| Inter-mouse distance | `compute_pairwise_distances` (centroids) | Mounting ⇒ the two mice are very close |
| Resident speed | `compute_speed` | Mounting ⇒ little locomotion of the resident |
| Resident→intruder orientation | `compute_forward_vector` + `compute_signed_angle_2d` | Resident faces the intruder's rear |
| Resident body length | neck→tail_base distance | Hunched-over posture shortens the body |

```{.python}
# Assemble features into a frame-by-feature table
X = pd.DataFrame({
    "inter_mouse_distance": ...,
    "resident_speed": ...,
    "relative_orientation": ...,
    "resident_body_length": ...,   # neck -> tail_base (more reliable than nose)
})
y = ds.is_mount.values
```

::: {.callout-note}
We use the **neck→tail_base** distance rather than nose→tail_base, because the neck is
tracked more reliably than the nose.
:::

## Explore the features

Plot each feature's distribution split by `mount` vs. non-`mount` frames. This shows
which features are discriminative, and makes the **class imbalance** obvious: mounting
occupies only a small fraction of frames.

```{.python}
# Overlaid histograms / violin plots of each feature, grouped by y
```

## Train / validation split (temporal, not random)

We split the single video **in time**: train on roughly the first 70% of frames,
validate on the last ~30%.

::: {.callout-important title="Why not a random split?"}
Adjacent frames are almost identical, so a *random* split would put near-duplicate
frames in both sets. The model would appear to score brilliantly while having
essentially memorised its neighbours — **information leakage**. A temporal split keeps
train and validation genuinely separate.

Note the naming: this held-out tail is a **validation** set, not a test set. As soon as
we inspect its scores and adjust features or thresholds to improve them, it has
influenced our choices. The honest **test** comes later, on a brand-new video
the model never saw (see [The real test](#the-real-test-a-new-video) below).
:::

```{.python}
split = int(0.7 * len(X))
X_train, X_val = X.iloc[:split], X.iloc[split:]
y_train, y_val = y[:split], y[split:]
```

## Train a random forest

A `RandomForestClassifier` is a solid, low-fuss baseline for tabular features. We set
`class_weight="balanced"` so the rare `mount` class is not swamped by the majority.

```{.python}
clf = RandomForestClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=0)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

## Evaluate on the validation set

Report **precision, recall and F1** for the `mount` class, plus a confusion matrix —
not plain accuracy.

::: {.callout-warning title="Accuracy lies under imbalance"}
If mounting is 5% of frames, a model that always predicts "not mount" scores 95%
accuracy while catching zero mounts. Precision/recall tell the real story.
:::

```{.python}
# classification_report(y_val, clf.predict(X_val))
# ConfusionMatrixDisplay ...
# clf.feature_importances_  -> which features carry the signal?
```

## From frame predictions to behaviour bouts

Per-frame predictions are noisy (isolated flipped frames). We **post-process** them
into clean bouts: fill short gaps, drop very short detections, then overlay the
predicted bouts against the BORIS ground-truth bouts on a timeline. This connects back
to the bout-style annotations from @sec-boris.

```{.python}
# smooth predictions -> merge into [start, stop] bouts -> timeline plot vs ground truth
```

## The real test: a new video

Now we apply the trained model to a **different** video it has never seen — with its own
BORIS ground-truth annotations (provided). We compute the same features, predict, and
compare.

Expect the scores to **drop** relative to validation. That gap is the honest measure of
how well the model generalises, and a teaching moment in itself: differences in lighting,
animals, and behaviour between videos (**domain shift**), combined with training on a
single video and few positive examples, all hurt generalisation.

```{.python}
# load new video's tracks + BORIS labels -> same feature pipeline -> clf.predict -> metrics
```

## Good practice, limitations, and where to go next

What we would do to build a classifier worth trusting:

- **More data**: many videos, multiple animals, and ideally multiple annotators (and
  measure inter-annotator agreement).
- **Better validation**: cross-validation that splits by *video*, never mixing frames
  from one video across folds.
- **Richer features**: rolling-window summaries (mean/std over short time windows),
  more keypoint relationships — closer to how tools like SimBA and MARS operate.
- **Handle imbalance** deliberately (class weights, resampling, threshold tuning on the
  precision/recall trade-off).
- **Off-the-shelf tools** built for this: [SimBA](https://github.com/sgoldenlab/simba),
  [MARS](https://github.com/neuroethology/MARS),
  [DeepEthogram](https://github.com/jbohnslav/deepethogram),
  [keypoint-MoSeq](https://keypoint-moseq.readthedocs.io/), and
  [A-SOiD](https://github.com/YttriLab/A-SOID).

::: {.callout-tip title="Discuss"}

- Which feature was most important? Does that match your intuition about mounting?
- How could you improve performance *without* collecting more data?
- The validation score was optimistic compared to the new-video test. Why? Where else
  in an ML pipeline can this kind of leakage sneak in?
:::
